lead: Transmission parameters, also called ABCD or chain parameters, give the input voltage and current of a two-port in terms of the output voltage and the current that flows out to the load. They were first used for telephone and power lines, where the sending-end quantities are wanted from the receiving-end ones. Their real strength is the cascade: when the output of one two-port feeds the input of the next, the overall ABCD matrix is simply the product of the individual matrices.
prereq: You need the port variables and their directions, Z and Y parameters, and 2 × 2 matrix multiplication.

sections.h3: The chain equations and the minus sign

blocks.text: The free pair is the output voltage V₂ and the current that leaves port 2 towards the load. I₂ is defined entering port 2, so the leaving current is −I₂:
V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂,   I₁ = CV₂ − DI₂
blocks.where: where A and D are pure numbers, B is in ohms and C is in siemens; in matrix form [V₁; I₁] = [T][V₂; −I₂] with [T] = [A B; C D].

blocks.text: The minus sign belongs to the definition, not to the network. Books that draw the output current leaving port 2 write V₁ = AV₂ + BI₂′ with I₂′ = −I₂; the numbers A, B, C and D are the same either way. What changes the numbers is keeping the entering current and dropping the minus sign.

Three building blocks are worth knowing by heart: a series impedance Z gives [1 Z; 0 1], a shunt admittance Y gives [1 0; Y 1], and an ideal transformer of turns ratio n : 1 gives [n 0; 0 1/n]. Each has AD − BC = 1. The transformer has no Z or Y matrix at all, so ABCD is the only one of these sets that can describe it.

sections.h3: Terminated two-port and inverse transmission parameters

blocks.text: With a load Z<sub>L</sub> at port 2, V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub>. Dividing the two chain equations gives the input impedance:

The limits give the four tests back: an open load (Z<sub>L</sub> → ∞) gives A/C, which equals z₁₁, and a shorted load gives B/D, which equals 1/y₁₁. The voltage gain is V₂/V₁ = Z<sub>L</sub>/(AZ<sub>L</sub> + B), and with the load open it is 1/A.

The inverse transmission parameters run the other way: V₂ = A′V₁ − B′I₁ and I₂ = C′V₁ − D′I₁. Inverting [T] gives A′ = D/ΔT, B′ = B/ΔT, C′ = C/ΔT, D′ = A/ΔT, with ΔT = AD − BC. For a reciprocal network ΔT = 1, so A′ = D, B′ = B, C′ = C and D′ = A.

Connect port 2 of network a to port 1 of network b. Then V₂<sub>a</sub> = V₁<sub>b</sub>, and the current leaving a is the current entering b: −I₂<sub>a</sub> = I₁<sub>b</sub>. The output vector of a is the input vector of b, so

blocks.where: where the matrix nearest the source is on the left. In full: A = A<sub>a</sub>A<sub>b</sub> + B<sub>a</sub>C<sub>b</sub>, B = A<sub>a</sub>B<sub>b</sub> + B<sub>a</sub>D<sub>b</sub>, C = C<sub>a</sub>A<sub>b</sub> + D<sub>a</sub>C<sub>b</sub>, D = C<sub>a</sub>B<sub>b</sub> + D<sub>a</sub>D<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.text: Order matters: [Tb][Ta] describes the circuit turned round. Any ladder can be built as a product of series and shunt blocks, which is how the second worked example rebuilds the T network. Series and parallel connections, and the conditions they need, are in interconnection of two-ports.

examples.question: Find the ABCD parameters of the T network with Z₁ = 2 Ω, Z₂ = 3 Ω and Z₃ = 4 Ω from the open and short tests at port 2, and check AD − BC.
steps: Port 2 open (I₂ = 0): I₁ flows through Z₁ and Z₃, so V₁ = 6I₁ and V₂ = 4I₁.
Port 2 shorted (V₂ = 0): V₁ = I₁(2 + 3 ∥ 4) = (26/7)I₁, and the current into the short is −I₂ = I₁ × 4/7.

examples.question: Build the same T network as a cascade of a 2 Ω series arm, a 0.25 S shunt arm and a 3 Ω series arm. Multiply the matrices, then find the input impedance with a 10 Ω load and check it by series-parallel reduction.
steps: Blocks: series 2 Ω = [1 2; 0 1], shunt 0.25 S = [1 0; 0.25 1], series 3 Ω = [1 3; 0 1].
Check: Z₂ + Z<sub>L</sub> = 13 Ω, in parallel with Z₃: 13 × 4/17 = 3.0588 Ω; add Z₁: 5.0588 Ω ✓.
examples.answer: [T] = [1.5 6.5 Ω; 0.25 S 1.75], Z<sub>in</sub> = 5.0588 Ω and V₂/V₁ = 0.4651 with the 10 Ω load.

traps: Keep the minus sign: V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂. Writing +BI₂ with I₂ entering flips the signs of B and D, and the cascade product then comes out wrong.
A and C come from the open-output test, B and D from the short-output test. Mixing them gives B = V₁/(−I₂) measured with port 2 open, where I₂ = 0 and the ratio is infinite.
B is in ohms and C in siemens; A and D have no unit. In the T network, B = 6.5 Ω and C = 0.25 S.
AD − BC = 1 tests reciprocity, not symmetry. The T network has AD − BC = 1 but A = 1.5 ≠ D = 1.75, so it is reciprocal and not symmetric.

Matrix order in a cascade follows the signal path: [T<sub>a</sub>][T<sub>b</sub>] with a nearest the source. [T<sub>b</sub>][T<sub>a</sub>] for the T network gives [1.75 6.5; 0.25 1.5], which is the network turned round.

quiz.q: Write the ABCD equations and the unit of each parameter.
quiz.a: V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂ and I₁ = CV₂ − DI₂, with I₂ entering port 2. A and D are pure numbers, B is in ohms, C in siemens.

quiz.q: Why is the output current written as −I₂ in the chain equations?
quiz.a: I₂ is defined entering port 2, but in a chain the current that matters is the one leaving port 2 and entering the next stage. Writing −I₂ makes the output vector of one stage equal the input vector of the next, so cascades multiply.

quiz.q: Give the ABCD matrices of a series impedance Z, a shunt admittance Y and an ideal n : 1 transformer.
A two-port has A = 2, B = 3 Ω, C = 1 S, D = 2. Find V₁ and I₁ when V₂ = 10 V with port 2 open.
quiz.a: I₂ = 0, so V₁ = AV₂ = 20 V and I₁ = CV₂ = 10 A.

quiz.q: With port 2 shorted, a two-port has V₁ = 6 V, I₁ = 4 A and I₂ = −2 A. Find B and D.
quiz.a: −I₂ = 2 A. B = V₁/(−I₂) = 3 Ω; D = I₁/(−I₂) = 2.

quiz.q: Find the inverse transmission parameters of the T network ([T] = [1.5 6.5; 0.25 1.75]).
quiz.a: Δ<sub>T</sub> = 1 (reciprocal), so A′ = D = 1.75, B′ = B = 6.5 Ω, C′ = C = 0.25 S, D′ = A = 1.5.

quiz.q: A reciprocal two-port has A = 1.5, B = 4 Ω and C = 0.5 S. Find D and say whether it is symmetric.
quiz.a: AD − BC = 1 gives D = (1 + 4 × 0.5)/1.5 = 2. Since A = 1.5 ≠ D = 2, it is not symmetric.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power engineers write a transmission line as V<sub>S</sub> = AV<sub>R</sub> + BI<sub>R</sub>, with sending-end and receiving-end quantities, and use the same A, B, C, D to classify short, medium and long lines. Microwave designers cascade line sections with ABCD matrices whose entries are cosh γl and sinh γl. Search for “ABCD parameters of a transmission line” and “nominal π model”.
